extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic/philosophy (interested in meaning, categories, and ontology)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length account of how names relate to the things they denote, with a proposed enumeration and distinctions among classes of namable things (feelings, substances, attributes) and discussion of ambiguous uses of names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is said to be relative, when, over and above the object which it denotes, it implies in its signification the existence of another object, also deriving a denomination from the same fact which is the ground of the first name. Or (to express the same meaning in other words) a name is relative, when, being the name of one thing, its signification can not be explained but by mentioning another. Or ... when the name can not be employed in discourse so as to have a meaning, unless the name of some other thing than what it is itself the name of, be either expressed or understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'father' connotes a fact regarded as an attribute of A while 'son' connotes the same fact as an attribute of B. The existence of a fact involving two individuals allows an attribute grounded on that fact to be ascribed to either individual. Relative names therefore presuppose or imply reference to a correlated object; without that other object the relative-name connotation would be swept away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal, æquivocal, and analogical (metaphorical) uses of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal, or applied univocally, with respect to all things of which it can be predicated in the same sense; it is æquivocal, or applied æquivocally, as respects those things of which it is predicated in different senses. An intermediate case is that of a name used analogically or metaphorically: predicated of two things not exactly in the same signification, but in significations somewhat similar, one being derivative from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'file' (tool) vs 'file' (line of soldiers) are truly different words accidentally coinciding in sound; 'brilliant light' vs 'brilliant achievement' are analogical uses. Beware fallacious reasoning that treats a metaphorical use as if it were literal — arguing from a metaphorical expression as if it were the original literal meaning is a common source of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerating the classes of Things capable of being predicates (Categories / Predicaments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic requires an enumeration of Existences as the basis for predication: the older school enumerated summa genera (Categories or Predicaments) believed to be the highest predicates capable of being affirmed of any namable thing. The traditional list (from Aristotle/schoolmen) is: Substantia, Quantitas, Qualitas, Relatio, Actio, Passio, Ubi, Quando, Situs, Habitus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author critiques this classification as rude, redundant and defective: some objects (e.g., sensations, states of mind) are omitted or misplaced; distinctions such as Quando vs Ubi vs Situs are ill-drawn. Use such lists with caution because they may both repeat and omit important kinds of namable things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding misleading general terms for existence (being/entity/essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many concrete names corresponding to the most general abstract term 'Existence' are ambiguous — 'thing', 'being', 'entity', 'essence' each carry tendencies to connote substances rather than all that exists. 'Being' tends to be synonymous with substance; 'entity' and 'essence' have been transformed in use and may imply separate or self-existent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When more precise words are lacking, choose whichever term on each occasion is least likely to mislead; do not pretend to use any such general term with rigorous adherence to a single sense. Warns that philosophical language will retain vagueness and that a writer should employ imperfect terms carefully to avoid misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Feelings (States of Consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings (or states of consciousness) are a primary leading division of namable things. A Feeling is a genus whose subordinate species are Sensation, Emotion, Thought, and Volitions (acts of the will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions/clarifications: Thought = what is internally conscious when we think (mental images, ideas, beliefs), distinct from the external object of thought; Sensation = what we are directly conscious of (e.g., white), distinct from the object causing it and from the attribute ascribed to the object; Volitions = acts of will which often form part of the connotation of relational names. Use these species to distinguish kinds of namable mental states in logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensation, object, and attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sensation is to be carefully distinguished from the object which causes the sensation, and from the attribute (quality) which we ascribe to the object in consequence of its exciting the sensation. Language often uses the same word for object, attribute, and sensation (e.g., 'white', 'color').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when analyzing propositions: the sensation (mental event), the external object, and the attribute ascribed to the object are different kinds of things. Because language often conflates them, a logical inquiry must separate these to avoid confusion (e.g., 'color' may denote sensation, attribute, or the object's property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensations and the bodily states that precede them
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish the sensation itself (a state of mind) from the state of the bodily organs which precedes the sensation and constitutes the physical agency producing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophically there is no firm foundation for dividing feelings into 'bodily' and 'mental' as if they are the same kind of thing; sensations are states of the sentient mind, while bodily organ states are physical facts not directly conscious. This helps avoid category mistakes when analyzing psychological or logical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as an act (recognition) and as a form of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception, according to some writers, consists in the recognition of an external object as the exciting cause of the sensation and is taken to be an act of the mind (an intuitive belief), whereas sensation is passive reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the purposes of logic, such perceptions are to be classed among feelings or states of mind (forms of belief). The legitimacy or conditions of intuitive perception belong to metaphysics/psychology rather than to logic; treat claims of intuitive perception as beliefs whose laws are external to formal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volitions and the constitution of actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Volitions (acts of the will) are active states of mind and form a principal part of the connotation of many relational names. An action is not one thing but a series of two things: the state of mind called a volition, followed by an effect. The volition + resulting physical effect together constitute the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analysis when considering names that connote actions (e.g., sovereign/subject, mortgagor/mortgagee): the connotation often includes actions actual, possible, or contingent, and sometimes actions performed by third parties (e.g., what a court would do to enforce an obligation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance vs Attribute (grammatical criterion and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: School logicians distinguish an attribute as something that must be the attribute 'of' something (e.g., color is the color of something) whereas a substance is self-existent and need not be followed by 'of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author critiques this as unsatisfactory: it pushes the explanatory burden onto the particle 'of' and fails to capture metaphysical distinctions. Use deeper metaphysical accounts (bodies/minds) rather than relying solely on grammatical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of body (substance) as the external cause of sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: A body, according to the received doctrine of modern metaphysicians, may be defined: the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations. Our conception of a body consists of a number of sensations habitually occurring together (a complex idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the opposing idealist view that what we call bodies may be only sets of sensations bound by law, and the realist reply that belief in external bodies is intuitive. For logical purposes, clarify whether one is treating 'body' as a theoretical substratum (matter) or as the systematic conjunction of possible sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenal/epistemic principle: all we know of objects are sensations and their order
rubrics_metrics.description: A central point (endorsed as important even by empiricist and Kantian writers) is that all we know of objects is the sensations which they give us, and the order of the occurrence of those sensations; the 'thing in itself' remains unknowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this epistemic caution in logical and epistemological analysis: claims about the 'real nature' of things beyond phenomenal representation are speculative; logical treatment should restrict itself to what is given in representation (sensations and their lawful order).
